blocks.text: **Logical reasoning** tests the ability to analyse information, spot patterns and draw valid conclusions. It spans **syllogisms, statements-and-conclusions/assumptions, cause-and-effect, seating arrangements and analogies** — the analytical backbone of the CSAT paper.

rows: Validity of conclusions from premises; use **Venn diagrams** (all/some/no).
What is taken for granted; an assumption must be **implicit**, not stated.
Only what **definitely follows** from the statement.
Linear/circular puzzles; draw a diagram, fix definite clues first.
Find the relationship (A:B :: C:?) or the **odd one out**.

items: **Read carefully** — note words like 'all', 'some', 'none', 'only', 'unless'.
**Diagram it** — Venn for syllogisms, sketches for arrangements.
**Test each option** by elimination; beware of assuming facts not given.
**Conclusion must follow strictly** — do not use outside knowledge.

sections.heading: 🧩 Methods & solved examples: logical & analytical reasoning

items: **Syllogisms**: use Venn diagrams; 'All A are B', 'Some', 'No'; a conclusion is valid only if it holds in EVERY possible diagram; 'possibility' vs 'definite'.
**Statement–assumption/argument/conclusion**: an assumption is something taken for granted; a strong argument is relevant + logical.
**Seating arrangement & puzzles**: draw the layout (linear/circular), note directions (facing centre = left/right reversed), fix definite clues first.
**Direction sense**: N-E-S-W; use Pythagoras for shortest distance; turns (left/right) relative to facing.
**Ordering/ranking**: 'from top = from bottom' → total = (rank from top + rank from bottom − 1).

blocks.text: Solved: In a row of 40, a boy is 12th from the left; his rank from the right = 40−12+1 = **29th**. || Facing north, turn right then right → now facing **south**.

prelimsPointers: **Syllogism** — use **Venn diagrams**; 'some A are B' does not mean 'some B are not A'.
**Assumption** = something **implicit/taken for granted** (not stated).
**Conclusion** = must **definitely follow** from the statement alone.
For **arrangement puzzles**, fix the most definite clue first, then build.
**Analogy** — identify the exact relationship before choosing.
Avoid bringing in **real-world knowledge** — judge only from given data.
Total = **(rank from top + rank from bottom − 1)**.
**Syllogism**: valid only if true in every Venn possibility; watch 'some'/'possibility'.
Circular table facing centre → **left/right are reversed** vs facing outward.
Direction shortest distance via **Pythagoras**.

glossary.definition: A logic problem deducing a conclusion from two or more given premises.
Something implicitly taken for granted in a statement, not explicitly stated.
A reasoning task requiring you to find a relationship of the form A:B :: C:?

blocks.text: A **number series** follows a hidden rule; the task is to find the **next term or the missing/wrong term**. Common patterns are **arithmetic, geometric, squares/cubes, alternating and mixed** progressions.

items: **Check the differences** between consecutive terms first.
If differences aren't constant, **check ratios** (×) or second differences.
Look for **squares, cubes, primes** or **±alternating** operations.
For a wrong-term question, find the rule that fits **most** terms.

sections.heading: 🧩 Methods & solved examples: number & letter series

items: Look for patterns: **+/− constant, ×/÷, squares/cubes, primes, alternate series, differences of differences**.
**Letter series**: use position numbers A=1…Z=26; note **+/− shifts**, opposite letters (A↔Z, B↔Y — sum to 27), skips.
**Wrong-number series**: find the term breaking the pattern.
Mixed series alternate two rules; watch for **Fibonacci-type** (each = sum of previous two).

prelimsPointers: First check the **common difference** (arithmetic), then the **common ratio** (geometric).
Watch for **n², n³, prime numbers, factorials**.
**Alternating series** interleave two patterns — separate the odd & even positions.
'Difference of differences' constant → a **second-order** (quadratic) series.
For **odd-one-out**, find the single term breaking the dominant rule.
Memorise **squares to 30** and **cubes to 15** for speed.
Series patterns: **±constant, ×/÷, squares/cubes, primes, differences-of-differences, Fibonacci**.
Letters: **A=1…Z=26**; opposite pair sums to **27** (A↔Z).
n²+n gives 2,6,12,20,30…; check **alternate** two-rule series.
Wrong-number question = spot the term breaking the rule.

glossary.definition: A sequence with a constant difference between consecutive terms.
A sequence with a constant ratio between consecutive terms.

blocks.text: **Coding-decoding** disguises words/numbers by a rule; you must decode the logic to encode a new word. Common types are **letter-shifting, positional, substitution and number coding**.

rows: Assign numbers to letters by a pattern (e.g. sum of positions).
Letters ↔ symbols in a fixed key.

items: Write the **alphabet with positions (A=1…Z=26)** for reference.
Compare each coded letter with the original to find the **shift**.
Remember **opposite letters** sum to 27 (A↔Z, B↔Y…).
For substitution, **build the mapping table** from the given sentences.
**Letter-shift coding**: each letter moved by a fixed number (Caesar); e.g. +1: CAT→DBU.
**Number coding**: letters → position numbers, or a rule (×2, +3).
**Substitution coding**: words stand for other words (e.g., 'sky=blue').
**Symbol/conditional coding**: apply given letter-symbol rules stepwise.
Method: compare the plain & coded words letter-by-letter to deduce the rule.

blocks.text: Solved: If CAT→DBU (each +1), then DOG → **EPH**. || If in a code A=1, B=2… then 'CAB' = **3-1-2**. || If TEACHER is coded VGCEJGT (+2), then LEARN → **NGCTP**.

prelimsPointers: **A=1 … Z=26**; opposite letters (A↔Z) sum to **27** (EJOTY trick: E=5, J=10, O=15, T=20, Y=25).
Find the **constant shift** by comparing coded and original letters.
For **substitution coding**, cross-map words across the given statements.
Number-coding often uses **position sums** or place values.
Note whether the shift is **forward (+)** or **backward (–)**.
Watch for **reversal** of the word plus a shift.
Common code = **fixed letter shift (Caesar +n)**; compare plain vs coded letter-by-letter.
Number coding often = **position value** (A=1…Z=26) or an arithmetic rule.
Substitution coding = words replaced by other words.
Solve conditional/symbol coding **step by step** per the given rules.

glossary.definition: Encoding by moving each letter a fixed number of places in the alphabet.
A memory aid marking letter positions E=5, J=10, O=15, T=20, Y=25 for quick reference.

blocks.text: **Blood-relation** problems test the ability to trace family relationships from clues (including coded relations and 'pointing-at-a-photo' puzzles). The key is to **draw a family tree** using clear symbols.

items: **Draw a tree**: put elder generation on top, younger below.
Mark **gender** and **generation** for every person.
For 'pointing' puzzles, resolve from the **speaker outward**.
Break coded relations (A+B, A×B) using the **given key** step by step.
Draw a **family tree**; use symbols: + male, − female, = couple, | generation link.
Key terms: paternal/maternal, in-laws, siblings, cousins, generations.
**Pointing/statement problems**: work outward from 'I/me'; 'my father's only son = myself'.
**Coded relations**: A+B (A is father of B), A−B, A×B per given symbols — decode stepwise.

blocks.text: Solved: 'Pointing to a man, a woman said, his mother is the only daughter of my mother' → the man is the woman's **son**. || 'My father's only son' = **myself**.

prelimsPointers: Always **draw a family tree** with gender and generation marked.
**Paternal** = father's side; **maternal** = mother's side.
In 'photo' puzzles, start from the speaker: 'my father's only son' = **himself** (if male).
**Generation gaps** — grandparent, parent, self, child, grandchild.
Solve **coded relations** strictly using the given symbol key.
Beware of gender-neutral clues (cousin, in-law, sibling).
Always **draw a family tree** (+male, −female, = couple).
'Father's only son / only daughter of my mother' clues resolve to **self/speaker**.
Decode **symbol relations** (A+B, A−B) step by step.
Track **generations** to avoid uncle/cousin errors.

glossary.definition: A diagram mapping family members by generation and gender to solve relation problems.
Relations on the father's side (paternal) versus the mother's side (maternal).

blocks.text: **Shapes & sub-sections** problems test **spatial/visual reasoning** — counting figures (triangles, squares) within a complex figure, identifying embedded shapes, completing figures, or counting how a figure is divided into parts.

rows: Count **smallest** units first, then combinations of 2, 3, 4… systematically.
Locate the given simple shape inside the complex one.
Choose the piece that completes the pattern/symmetry.
Count regions formed by intersecting lines.

items: **Label** each line/vertex to avoid missing or double-counting.
Count **smallest components first**, then progressively larger composites.
Use **symmetry** to speed counting.
Recount methodically — spatial questions reward care over speed.

sections.heading: 🧩 Methods & solved examples: figures, shapes & sub-sections

items: **Counting figures**: count systematically (all triangles/squares) — smallest first, then combinations; avoid double counting.
**Embedded/hidden figures**: find the given shape inside a complex one.
**Paper folding & cutting**: visualise symmetry — a fold doubles the cut pattern.
**Mirror & water images**: mirror = left-right flip; water = top-bottom flip.
**Dice & cubes**: opposite faces; if a cube (n×n×n) is painted & cut — corner cubes have 3 painted faces (8), edges 2 ((n−2)×12), faces 1 (6(n−2)²), inner 0 ((n−2)³).

blocks.text: Solved: A 3×3×3 painted cube cut into 27 → 3-face:8, 2-face:12, 1-face:6, 0-face:1. || Mirror image of 'b' looks like **'d'**.

prelimsPointers: Count the **smallest figures first**, then combinations — be systematic.
**Label vertices/lines** to avoid double-counting.
Exploit **symmetry** to multiply counts.
For completion/analogy figures, look for **rotation, reflection, addition/deletion**.
Practise standard figures (a triangle divided into rows gives a known count).
Painted cube (n³): 3-faces=**8**, 2-faces=**12(n−2)**, 1-face=**6(n−2)²**, 0-face=**(n−2)³**.
**Mirror** image = left-right flip; **water** image = top-bottom flip.
Count figures **systematically** (smallest → combinations).
Dice: identify **opposite faces** from two/three views.

glossary.definition: The ability to visualise and manipulate shapes and their arrangements mentally.
A simple shape hidden within a larger, more complex figure.

blocks.text: **Venn diagrams** represent relationships among sets using overlapping circles. They are used both for **logical relationships between groups** (e.g. doctors, women, players) and for **set-based counting** problems.

rows: All elements in A or B (or both).
Elements common to A and B.
Choose the diagram matching the group relation (e.g. all X are Y = circle inside circle).

items: For **relationship questions**, decide how the categories overlap (subset, disjoint, partial).
For **counting**, fill the **innermost region first**, then work outward.
Apply the **inclusion-exclusion formula** for unions.
'Only A' = n(A) minus all its overlaps.
**Venn diagrams** show set relations — union (∪), intersection (∩), complement.
**Class-relation**: choose the diagram matching real relationships (e.g., Dogs–Animals–Cats; Doctors–Men–Women).
**Set formula (2 sets)**: n(A∪B) = n(A)+n(B)−n(A∩B); **(3 sets)**: n(A∪B∪C)=n(A)+n(B)+n(C)−n(A∩B)−n(B∩C)−n(A∩C)+n(A∩B∩C).
**'Only'/'exactly' regions**: subtract overlaps carefully; use the diagram regions.

blocks.text: Solved: In a class of 50, 30 like tea, 25 coffee, 10 both → like at least one = 30+25−10 = **45**; neither = 50−45 = **5**.

prelimsPointers: **n(A∪B) = n(A) + n(B) – n(A∩B)** (two sets).
Three-set: **add singles, subtract pairs, add the triple**.
For counting, **start from the centre (all three)** and work outward.
'Exactly one', 'exactly two', 'at least one' need careful region-wise counting.
For relationship diagrams, match to 'all/some/no' logic (subset, overlap, disjoint).
**n(A∪B) = n(A)+n(B)−n(A∩B)**; extend the formula to 3 sets.
Pick the **Venn diagram matching real class relations** (e.g., Doctor-Man-Woman).
'Neither' = Total − n(A∪B).
Watch 'only A', 'exactly two' regions.

glossary.definition: The set of all elements in either set (A∪B).
The set of elements common to both sets (A∩B).
The principle for counting union sizes by adding singles and adjusting for overlaps.
